To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the physico-chemical parameters recognized to govern amyloids formation by partially and fully unfolded proteins in vitro can be used to predict the propensity to aggregate in the complex environment provided by a living cell.

we have shown that the physico-chemical parameters previously recognized as the main determinants of amyloid formation in vitro are largely applicable to the in vivo aggregation of folding-incompetent proteins in Escherichiacoli.
we identified the molecular determinants for amyloid formation by an unfolded protein expressed in vivo in a controlled manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of protein aggregation in living cells and with the search for the molecular factors governing this process.
the molecular mechanisms of protein folding and misfolding in the complex environment in which they occur in vivo.
the study of protein misfolding and aggregation in living organisms, and more in particular with the search for molecular determinants of aggregation in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the physico-chemical properties of the polypeptide chain are sufficient to predict the aggregation propensity of a given protein in vivo.
protein aggregation in vivo, as in vitro, is mainly driven by the physicochemical properties of the protein sequence, in particular its hydrophobicity and propensity to form beta-sheet structures.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the physico-chemical parameters previously recognized as governing amyloid formation by partially or fully unfolded proteins are largely valid in vivo and that the in vivo aggregation of a protein is a function of the intrinsic propensity of the unfolded protein to form amyloids and of the concentration at which the protein is expressed.
, at least for the proteins we have studied, the propensity to form amyloids is the most important factor governing protein aggregation in vivo.
the propensity of a protein to aggregate is a property that can be measured in vitro and is conserved in vivo, at least in E. coli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the physico-chemical parameters previously recognized as major determinants of amyloid formation in vitro are applicable also in vivo.
protein aggregation in vivo is not a random event but is governed by specific physicochemical properties of the aggregating protein.
, in vivo, the propensity to aggregate is not a unique and intrinsic feature of a single protein, but it depends on its relative concentration with respect to the cellular proteome.
